rect.title: RFC 8200 §7; carries DSCP and ECN (RFC 2474, RFC 3168)
octets of payload after this 40-octet header; any extension headers count as payload
8-bit selector, same values as the IPv4 Protocol field (IANA protocol numbers)
decremented by one per forwarding node; the packet is discarded at zero
128-bit address of the originator of the packet
128-bit address of the intended recipient; possibly not the ultimate recipient, if a Routing header is present

svg.metadata:
# FigDown — figures as text. Spec: https://github.com/FigDown/figdown
figdown 0.1 bitfield # IPv6 header — transcribed from the ASCII diagram in RFC 8200 §3 # (Deering & Hinden, July 2017), https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200.txt # # What this figure probes: a 128-bit field spanning four 32-bit rows. # # Fidelity rule for this file: it carries EXACTLY the fields RFC 8200 §3 # draws, and nothing else. Payload and extension headers follow on the wire # but sit outside that diagram, so they are not fields here — an extra row # would mean the .fd no longer reconstructs back to the RFC one for one. title "IPv6 header"
# `numbering=` is REQUIRED and has no default: a defaulted direction would # render a ruler asserting something false, and a wrong ruler looks exactly # like a right one. `msb0` is the IETF packet convention — bit 0 is the MSB, # ruler 0…31 left to right — which is what the "0 1 2 3 / 0 1 2 3 4 5 …" # scale above an RFC diagram means. `word=` is the row width in bits. bitfield ipv6 "IPv6 Header (RFC 8200 §3)" word=32 numbering=msb0
# Word 0 — 4 + 8 + 20 = 32 bits. field "Version" 4 description="4-bit Internet Protocol version number = 6" field "Traffic Class" 8 description="RFC 8200 §7; carries DSCP and ECN (RFC 2474, RFC 3168)" field "Flow Label" 20 description="RFC 8200 §6, RFC 6437"
# Word 1 — 16 + 8 + 8 = 32 bits. field "Payload Length" 16 description="octets of payload after this 40-octet header; any extension headers count as payload" field "Next Header" 8 description="8-bit selector, same values as the IPv4 Protocol field (IANA protocol numbers)" field "Hop Limit" 8 description="decremented by one per forwarding node; the packet is discarded at zero"
# Words 2–5, then words 6–9. 128 is wider than `word=32`, so each address # spans FOUR rows automatically and is still ONE field — and # it DRAWS as one: a single box, no rules between the four rows, the name # written once. RFC 8200 §3 draws the same fact by joining the four rows with # `+` rules instead of `+-+-+` bit rules, and this figure is that convention # in SVG. Splitting an address into four 32-bit pieces would assert four # fields on the wire that do not exist. # # The drawing is a courtesy; the `.fd` is the machine-readable truth either # way. A reading agent takes the count off the `field` line — one field, 128 # bits — never off the picture, so it answers "how wide is the source address" # identically whether the engine drew four joined rows or one tall box. field "Source Address" 128 fill=#dbeafe description="128-bit address of the originator of the packet" field "Destination Address" 128 fill=#dbeafe description="128-bit address of the intended recipient; possibly not the ultimate recipient, if a Routing header is present"
# 4+8+20 + 16+8+8 + 128 + 128 = 320 bits = the fixed 40 octets of RFC 8200 §3. # Every width is in the text, so a reader checks that sum without the picture.
